title: Is it safe to give an AI agent access to record your product?
summary: What access an AI recording agent needs, why a staging test account is the safe default, what repo access is for, and a checklist for security review.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- Giving an AI agent login access is safe when it signs in to a test account built for it, in staging, with a narrow role and sample data. The agent can only do what that account can do.
- The agent needs a login to your web app. Source code access is optional and is used to spot product changes that make videos outdated.
- For MFA, use an authenticator app or an inbox your team owns, never a person's phone.
- If you connect a repository, connect only the frontend one and read the permission screen before you approve it.
- [Clueso Agents](https://www.clueso.io/agents) are on the Enterprise plan. They sign in with logins saved in your Clueso workspace and never see the passwords or codes themselves.


In September, a buyer on one of our sales calls had just heard how our agent signs in to a product and records it on its own. Then the conversation reached what we'd need from their side, a login to their company's product, and they flagged a problem. Their IT team, they said, was "very reticent to hand out login credentials," and they would have vetting questions "that quite frankly are over my head."


Her call wasn't unusual. Over the past year, buyers have asked about giving an agent login credentials on more than 30 of our sales calls, and about source code access on roughly as many. The person asking is usually in customer education or product marketing, and they're the one who has to carry the answer to IT.


This post is that answer, written so you can forward it to your security reviewer. For the wider vendor review, including SSO and data residency, see our guide to[what enterprise buyers ask AI video vendors in security review](https://www.clueso.io/blog/evaluating-enterprise-ai-video-tools) .


## Is it safe to give an AI agent login access to record your product?


Giving an AI agent login access to record your product is safe when the agent signs in to an account created for it. That means a test account in a staging or demo environment, with a role limited to the screens it has to record and sample data you'd be happy to show a customer. The agent can only do what that account can do.


Most of the risk sits in that account choice. A recording agent signs in and clicks through the walkthrough you describe, the way a person would.


## What access does an AI recording agent need, and why?


Three kinds of access come up in these conversations, and only the login is always required.


Access


What the agent uses it for


Required?


A login to your web app


Signing in, following the walkthrough, and recording the screens


Yes


A second sign-in factor


Finishing sign-in on accounts that enforce MFA


Only if the test account has MFA turned on


A connection to your code repository


Spotting which product changes affect existing videos, and suggesting updates


No


The agent sees your product the way a user with that role sees it, so the role decides what ends up on screen. An end-user account produces end-user footage, which is usually what a customer-facing tutorial should show anyway.


## Should the agent use a staging account or a production account?


Use a dedicated test account in a staging or demo environment unless you have a specific reason not to. Staging keeps the agent away from real customer records, and anything it changes there costs you nothing. Three decisions shape the account.


**Give the agent its own identity.** Create a named account for it instead of lending it someone's login. If that person leaves and their account is disabled, the recordings stop. A shared login also makes it impossible to tell the agent's clicks from the person's in your own access logs.


**Give it the narrowest role that reaches the screens you film.** NIST defines[least privilege](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/least_privilege) as restricting access "to the minimum necessary to accomplish assigned tasks," and a recording agent is a clean case for it. If your videos show an end user's workflow, an end-user role is enough. Keep a separate admin-level test account for the admin tutorials, in staging only.


**Fill the account with realistic sample data.** An empty account makes a poor video, because dashboards render blank and lists have nothing to click. Seed it with fictitious names and figures that look like real use, so the footage teaches something and there's nothing to redact afterwards. If something sensitive still slips into a frame, here's[how to blur part of a video](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-blur-part-of-a-video) .


### What about SSO and MFA?


If staging enforces MFA, give the agent's account a factor it can use with nobody present. Authenticator-app codes work because the setup key can be stored with the saved login, and emailed codes work if they go to a group inbox your team controls. A push approval or an SMS code to someone's phone needs that person every time the agent signs in.


SSO needs a decision from whoever owns your identity provider. One route is a dedicated identity for the agent, assigned to the test app only and protected by an authenticator app. The other is a local password login on the staging tenant, switched on for the test account alone.


## What does an AI agent do with access to your source code?


Repository access is the part security teams push back on hardest. On one of our calls, a buyer said plainly that "any production repo is going to be a no."


An agent that reads your frontend code can see which screens a release touched and match them to the videos that show those screens. That lets it flag an outdated video the day a change merges, instead of the day a customer files a ticket about a menu that moved.


Without repository access, the agent still records from its login. You lose automatic detection, so someone on your team decides when a video needs re-recording. With monthly releases, that's a short review after each one. Daily releases are much harder to review by hand, and that's where detection saves the most time.


If you do connect one, connect only the frontend repository. If your frontend shares a monorepo with your backend, raise it with the vendor first, because repository access would then cover both. GitHub lets you[review an installed app's permissions and limit which repositories it can see](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/using-github-apps/reviewing-and-modifying-installed-github-apps) , and your reviewer should compare the requested scopes with what the vendor says it does with the code.


## What should a security reviewer check before approving an AI recording agent?


Your IT team can confirm the first four rows before the vendor is involved at all.


Check


What a safe setup looks like


Account


A dedicated test account for the agent, not a person's login or a shared admin


Environment


Staging or demo, filled with fictitious data


Role


The narrowest role that reaches the screens being recorded


MFA


An authenticator app or a team-owned inbox, never a person's phone


Credential storage


Encrypted, scoped to your workspace, and never shown to the AI model or written to logs


Repository access


Optional; frontend repository only; requested scopes match the stated use


Actions in the account


Your team writes or approves each walkthrough, and someone reviews the video before it's published


Run history


A log of each agent run you can match against your own access logs


Revocation


You can rotate the password or disable the account yourself, at any time


Deletion


Saved logins are deleted when you remove them or close the workspace


## What should you ask any vendor whose agent records your product?


A security reviewer can't approve an answer someone gave on a call. Ask for these in writing, and match each answer to a row in the checklist.


1. Where are saved logins stored, how are they encrypted, and which of your staff can read them?
2. Does the AI model ever see the password or one-time code, or does your system fill them in?
3. Is the sign-in step kept out of the recordings and out of your logs?
4. What does the agent do if a walkthrough includes deleting or submitting something?
5. Where does the agent's browser run, and is that provider on your published sub-processor list?
6. If we connect a repository, which scopes do you request, do you keep a copy of our code, and for how long?
7. Can we see a log of every agent run?
8. How long do you keep raw recordings, and what happens to them when we delete a project?
9. How do we revoke the agent's access in an emergency?


## How does Clueso handle agent logins and repository access?


[Clueso Agents](https://www.clueso.io/agents) are on the Enterprise plan. The browser agent signs in to your product with logins saved in your Clueso workspace, including authenticator-app codes and emailed one-time codes, and it never sees the passwords or codes themselves. Clueso asks for credentials to a demo or staging account, and your workspace can give the agent its own written instructions, for every login or for specific ones.


Saved logins belong to your workspace and are deleted with it, and Clueso[encrypts data in transit and at rest](https://www.clueso.io/faqs) on every plan. Each agent run shows up in the workspace's Recordings log with its status, and the result arrives as an editable draft, with a narrated video and a[step-by-step guide](https://www.clueso.io/features/help-articles) , so nothing goes out until someone on your team has reviewed it.


Repository access is optional. Clueso connects to GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket, needs only your frontend repository, and doesn't modify your code. With a repository connected,[Auto Updates](https://www.clueso.io/features/auto-updates) , a paid add-on on Enterprise, checks each push against the flows your videos cover and flags the videos it made outdated. Without one, the agent still records from the demo login.


## Frequently asked questions


### Is it safe to give an AI video agent login access to record our product?


Yes, if the login belongs to a test account built for the agent, with a narrow role and fictitious data. Clueso asks for a demo or staging login, saves it in your workspace, and the agent never sees the password or one-time codes.[Clueso Agents](https://www.clueso.io/agents) are on the Enterprise plan.


### Do AI tools that auto-update product videos need access to our source code?


Not to record, but usually to detect changes on their own. Clueso's agent records from a login alone. Connecting your frontend repository on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket lets[Auto Updates](https://www.clueso.io/features/auto-updates) , a paid Enterprise add-on, flag the videos a push made outdated, and Clueso doesn't modify your code.


### Can an AI agent log in to a product that uses SSO or MFA?


For MFA, use an authenticator app or emailed codes to an inbox your team owns, because push and SMS approvals need a person. Clueso's agent supports authenticator-app codes and emailed one-time codes. For SSO, agree a dedicated test identity or a local staging login with whoever runs your identity provider.


### Will the agent change data in our account?


A recording agent clicks what the walkthrough tells it to click, so a walkthrough that deletes something will do it. That's why the test account matters. In Clueso, your workspace can give the agent written instructions for each login, and every video arrives as an editable draft you review before it's published, per the[Clueso Agents FAQ](https://www.clueso.io/agents) .


### What happens to the saved login if we stop using the tool?


Disable the test account or rotate its password on your side, then ask the vendor to delete the saved login. In Clueso, saved logins belong to your workspace and are deleted along with it, and the[FAQ](https://www.clueso.io/faqs) explains how admins delete a workspace.


Before your next vendor call, ask your IT team to create the agent's account first: a named identity in staging, an end-user role, sample data, and an authenticator-app factor. Then send the vendor the nine questions above and ask for written answers before the security review is booked. Your reviewer then signs off on one specific login, with its role and data already known.
